utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present. Presentation as yesterday with the exception of Ms. Tapuskovic for the Popovic Defence team. So good morning to you, Mr. McCloskey. And good morning to you, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, no, you can remain standing, it's going to take very little time. You had your motion for the admission of a number of documents from the bar table. It has been responded to in a positive manner by the Prosecution and therefore we are hereby granting your motion. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yesterday we ended with 65 ter 4236, which I don't think we need to put up on the screen. We saw a reference in that March 2nd Zvornik regular combat report to: "At around 8.30 hours, columns of civilians and soldiers with pack animals were noticed from Udrc and Rasevo towards Konjevic Polje. The columns were hit with every available means." I think we talked about that a bit. But now going on to 65 ter 4258, which is the daily combat report of the corps and to the Main Staff. And if we can go down and it's in paragraph 1, the second paragraph of the-- entitled, "The enemy." We see the same phrase going up to the Main Staff, but it has left out the part about civilians. Were you told by the corps not to shell civilians? Or fire upon civilians as a result of this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why the corps worded this document as they did. This was a column moving from Tuzla towards Konjevic Polje with pack animals, and obviously, they were carrying the ammunition and weapons for the forces deployed in the area of Konjevic Polje. And that was one of the reasons why fire was opened. We never had an order to fire on civilians. And it was quite clear that we were expected only to target military facilities. And this column was a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was, General, we see that they've left out civilians in their report. Did the corps tell you to stop firing at civilians?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, they did not tell me either to shoot at civilians or not to shoot at civilians. What we did here, we opened fire at this particular column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they tell you not to put in your reports that you were firing at civilians?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Since they didn't tell me either to open fire or not to open fire, therefore, I was not told to put -- what to put in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 4243.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a daily combat report of a colleague of yours, Lieutenant-Colonel Andric. It's dated 2 March. And he is describing the situation as he is involved in these activities, and we see in paragraph 2, as he is describing the movement of the forces that the village of Gobalji has been burnt and tomorrow the plan is to do Paljevine. So were you and Andric going down as -- after fighting the Muslims, were you burning these villages?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Villages were not being burned along the axis of my action, and by the way, I'm not familiar with the area where Mr. Andric was carrying out actions. Paljevine is a feature and I think you can see it in the map behind my back. It was on the axis of Andric's forces. As for the other village of Gobalji, I think that this was a mixed village and that it had already been burned. Whether that happened during a fighting or at some other time, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were open to the reality that Andric's forces just burnt that village?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that fact. It was an entirely different axis of attack. We just even couldn't see each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 4259.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This, again, is a Drina Corps report, the same day as Andric's report. I want to direct your attention to paragraph number 2 of this report of the Main Staff. Where it basically repeats what Andric has said but instead of saying the village was burnt, it says: "Part of the forces of the brigade liberated the village of Gobalji at the frontline in the area of Cerska." So now we see, as in your previous document, the editing going on. Can we conclude that "liberated" in this particular document actually means "burnt"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought I had solved it. You need to be patient with us, Mr. McCloskey, and all the others, because we have lost the -- but I don't know what is happening, there's something happening now. Something happening now. Okay. It seems to be working now. Did anyone else experience the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you solved it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sort of. I seem to have a transcript but not where I would expect to find it, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can anyone assist Mr. Haynes, please. Anybody else has the problem? Solved. Okay. My apologies to you, Mr. McCloskey, I had to stop you. So you need to go back to page 4, lines 5, or 5 to 9. That's where I stopped you. You had just read part of Exhibit 4259.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So General, we can conclude from looking at this Drina Corps report that when the Drina Corps says that this village has been liberated, it really means burnt; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot draw such a conclusion as you did. I know that there was a lot of fighting along this axis. There was a battalion from the Krajina Corps that between 15 and 20 soldiers died in the fighting. Some villages and some houses could have been burnt as a result of fighting. I know that on the slopes of Cerska, which was predominantly Muslim, there were yet some Serbian villages. The village that was mentioned later on in the secondary passage was the Serbian village, it was not burnt at the time but it was deserted. We chose axis of our attacks along the lines where the Serbian villages were situated because it was easier for us to advance in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you agree with me the Drina Corps has removed the term "burnt" and replaced it with "liberated"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have had a consultation with Andric and maybe his statement referred to this part of the Serbian village that had been burnt but I really don't know what actually transpired there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 4244.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another report from your colleague Andric, dated 2 March 1993, to the Drina Corps and what I'd like to draw your attention to is near the bottom at the English. It's B/C/S page 1. And he points out that -- and says: "In the course of the day, special units of the 1st Birac Brigade took and destroyed the village of Gobalji thus freeing up the left flank of the main forces and the attack on Cerska. At the entry into the village, our soldiers found weapons and other military equipment, as well as food and cattle, which the enemy left behind when fleeing from our forces. If the Zvornik Brigade continues the attack towards the above-mentioned facilities, Udrc will not be a threat anymore to a single unit." So we can conclude from this that you and Andric are working on the same operation in the similar vicinity; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the map behind me, you can see that Udrc is a feature at high elevation and covered in wood. It is a dominant feature. If we manage to capture it, we would have a tactical advantage. Andric and I did act together as part 1 operation, however, we were not close in combat. In his first part of the report, he said that he would be compelled to withdraw into his zone unless the forces of the Zvornik Brigade do not accelerate their actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we acted together in this operation, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 4245.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is March 4th, a couple of days later. This is a report from you in your name. It appears to say, we are not sure, Major Pandurevic, have you been promoted at this point or is ...

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was promoted on the 7th of January irrespective of any combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- looking at this, it's on the front page, and that the computer may be as good a view of this as the actual document. It's a little bigger, in fact. What I call your attention to is you describe the activities, and then you say under paragraph 1: "Activity in the direction of Konjevic Polje, Duge Njive," and some other villages, "and Glodi have been taken and facilities in Glodi burnt." Now Glodi was a Muslim town with a mosque. Did your units burn Glodi like it says here, the facilities in Glodi?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, back in November or even October, the entire area of Kamenica including Glodi was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. However, on the 6th and 7th November, the whole area including Bosansko Brdo fell and this village is located there. At the time when I was there, I didn't see any mosque and I honestly don't know which facilities they are referring to as being burnt. It might have been houses but it might have been some fortifications for housing firing positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, did you say you are not sure what "they" are referring to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you are referring to now. Maybe the translation was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The translation we got, General, is that after I asked you that question, you said, "I'm not sure what facilities they are referring to." But I can go on. You wrote this report or you -- went out under your name; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but when you'll speak about facility in military terms, that involves firing positions and cover. Whereas a house is a house. That's how it is called. When it is called in military terms, it's a facility. It could be a bunker, a shelter, and there were such facilities in Glodjansko Brdo and Glodi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you burn in Glodi?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm tell you can that houses in Glodi were not burned. This village was empty. You mentioned a mosque. I didn't see any mosque there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 4260.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This again is the Drina Corps report to the Main Staff on the same day and it we can see down it begins at page 1 in the B/C/S and it's at the bottom of page 1 in the English, but then -- it's at the bottom of page 1 in English. And it says: "Parts of the Zvornik Brigade liberated Duge Njive and Glodi." So again we see the term "burnt" left out. And my questions are the same, did the Drina Corps tell you not to burn or did they tell you not to say that you'd burned?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as to your previous question. My report says that facilities were burnt. It doesn't say specifically the houses or the village. Here it says liberated. When we launched an attack and took some facilities, we used to call it liberations and that is what the Muslims did as well. They said that they liberated Kravica and we said that we -- they said that they liberated Kravica and we said that we liberated Konjevic Polje. Even now if you walk through this village, you can see that the houses had not been burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you didn't burn any houses in this operation ever?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless there was fire coming from certain fortified buildings they might have been burned or set on fire by fire from weapons, and in that context, I do not rule out the possibility of any house being actually burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Accidental burning, you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 4247.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have amended or -- my answer. I didn't say accidently. In fighting, if you have a building or a facility from which fire is coming, then you target it deliberately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course. Okay. This is another report dated a few days later, March 10th, 1993, from -- I think you can see that from the original, I hope. And this is in your name. And you talk about the -- what has been happening in most of this. And we know you've had a chance to study this. Well, I can ask you that. Have you had a chance to study this document before I just handed it to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a CD or a DVD with all these reports, so I probably have read it, but not recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it says at the bottom -- you say at the bottom: "We propose that houses should not be torched when taking control of Konjevic Polje, but that they be inhabited by people from Tuzla and other areas."

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What people from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs, Serbian refugees who wanted to leave Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we can --

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who are already in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we can conclude from this that prior to your report, houses were being torched and wasted?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that on my axis of action, they were not. But when I emerged at these positions quoted here, I noticed that from the direction of Cerska, there was smoke and there was burning, and that's why I made this timely proposition to the corps command before we moved towards Konjevic Polje to do this or, rather, not to do this, because there were troops who followed from behind and did torch.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not quite sure about this last part. Could Mr. Pandurevic repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pandurevic, we have an interpretation but the interpreters are not quite sure they got it right. So I will read out to you what we have here and if it's correct, please say so. If you need to change it, please then go ahead. "I repeat that on my axis of action, they were not. But when I emerged at these positions quoted here, I noticed that from the direction of Cerska, there was smoke and there was burning, and that's why I made this timely proposition to the corps commander before we moved towards Konjevic Polje to do this or, rather, not to do this because there were troops who followed from behind and did torch."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't troops that followed from behind. It was the locals who used to live in that area. At the entrance to Konjevic Polje, from the direction of Drinjaca, there were several Serb houses before the war, and at that time they were burnt down. And those locals, when they returned, they would be prone to burning a few Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I should say that's precisely the correction I was advised should be made from my left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So none of your troops did any burning, it was all Serb locals?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say no one. It could have happened that there were soldiers whose villages used to be there before. But when the unit passed through Konjevic Polje, I set up a police check-point at the entrance to Konjevic Polje to prevent any of the locals from the Zvornik municipality from coming into that area and to loot and take away some property, that was the Bratunac municipality. And I know that some people took a round-about way from the surrounding hills on tractors and one person even got killed travelling that way. The houses remained intact. One of my escorts once took an aerial cable because he said he needed it for his TV set, and I said I'll hang you with that cable if you try to take it from here. None of my men took anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So then the previous references to -- that Andric made to burning things and that you made to burning facilities which got left out of the Drina Corps reports, we should just ignore that and we should put this burning on local Serbs, is that what you are telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the soldiers are responsible under the command of an officer, in this case Andric, or the responsibility lies on local Serbs, I don't know. Maybe both are responsible. But one thing is true, both things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But Vinko Pandurevic is not responsible?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said, Mr. McCloskey. If fighting is going on for some features, houses, buildings holding soldiers of the BH Army, and if they are firing from these buildings at us, those are military targets. We open fire at them, we throw grenades, we fire shells. And then the building can be burnt down. However, if a soldier set something on fire when the fighting is over and if I am aware of that, then it's my responsibility. To that extent, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to a UN report now of the same time-period, 13 -- 65 ter 4252, to get just a glimpse into what the UN is reporting. And we don't have a translation of this so I think we are going to need to look at the screen. Actually, we did get one. It did come in in time. So it should be -- well, it's page 2 of the English, but if we can stay with page 1 for a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've seen these sorts of things. It's to the headquarters of Zagreb from the HQ command in Kiseljak and it's describing the general situation in various sectors. And the sector that I'm concerned about is on page 2, and it's the Tuzla sector --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to that. Page 1 of the B/C/S. I think we need to go back in the B/C/S. Page 1 in B/C/S, page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And under the Tuzla section --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And perhaps, yeah, if you could blow that up for the General so he can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The part I want to draw your attention to is -- it begins a few lines down: "The first report of an attack by the BSA on the village of Konjevic Polje came through at 1124 hours. Shelling and reports of the attack failed to disperse the hundreds of civilians that had surrounded the BritBat party. At 1412 hours, OC B SQN 9/12 stated that he was reconsidering his options and at 1424 hours requested that Major Pandurevic (the local BSA commander at Zvornik) be urged to stop the shelling as civilians were being caught in the fire. At 1450A hours, one round landed killing 2 civilians and injuring three children under the age of 6, two of which lost their legs. At 1530 hours, word was received from BH C Kiseljak that the BSA was in the process of checking fire. The request for a safe route out of BritBat was also being considered. "At 1545 hours, information came through that the Spartan was being towed by the Foden and that the Sultan and the Land Rover were about 300 metres apart and still surrounded by civilians. At 1619 hours, the Foden received an indirect hit with shrapnel going through its radiator. At 1642 hours, another round landed in the group of civilians by the Foden, killing 10. No BritBat injuries. It was also decided at this time to abandon the Foden and Spartan and move north towards Zvornik. Because of the frequency change, at 1700 hours coms with C B SQN were lost. It was assumed that the group was still moving. "At 1905 hours, it was reported that OC B SQN was in conference with the BiH. This was assumed to be the edge of what remains of the Cerska pocket. Permission was granted to carry on and word has passed to Major Pandurevic that the BritBat group would shortly be approaching the BSA lines." Do you recall this incident where this --

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's dated 13 March 1993. Reporting on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember these details. The artillery of the Zvornik Brigade could not observe its own fire from the positions where it was and we never fired randomly. We never did that. From what direction this fire came and whether it came from the direction it says here, I don't know, but I know this gentleman was interested in me because he was supposed to come to Zvornik and come close to our positions. And I remember one group of military observers, among them a British officer, one Russian officer, and one other officer, Australian or a Belorussian, I'm not sure. They went to that area and returned awhile later. And as for artillery fire by us at Konjevic Polje, it was never random. We never fired without observing, and we were simply unable to observe that location. So I'm not aware of these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would suggest to you this was not random artillery. This was deliberately designed to drop these artillery rounds right on the crowd. You can tell me nothing else about this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not deliberately designed because how could I know where people are in that broad space if I can't see that space and have no information. On top of that, I was perfectly aware that military observers were headed there. I wouldn't fire on them. Fire could have come from some other direction by someone else who didn't know that the military observers were headed there. And at that time I didn't receive any protests from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Who else could have been firing artillery at -- in the direction of BritBat and the Muslim population in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of BritBat you are talking about. There was no BritBat there that I know. However, fire was possible from Cerska and from Kasaba directions. From both of these locations it is easier to observe the area of Konjevic Polje than from Zvornik of because there a mountain chain between -- between Zvornik and Konjevic Polje along the Drinjaca River that prevents you from seeing Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on. You talked a bit in your direct about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It might be significant, but I think the three letters SQN are short for "squadron" not "son," and that may actually be important as to what sort of size of force from the British army were in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can probably sort out those abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you spoke in direct about your dealings with General Morillon. It was this time-period, as we know, March 1993. You had mentioned, on page 30808, that: "I was honoured to maintain contacts with a high-ranking general."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let me go to 65 ter 4250.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've highlighted the part I'm going to ask you about. It's on page 2 of the English. And we can see that this is another report from you on March 11th, it's the time-frame that I'm sure you will agree that you were dealing with General Morillon and others. And you talk about the situation. And then on line 9 you say: "Due to the bigger presence of UNPROFOR, different humanitarian organisations and other bitangi," which is translated as "good-for-nothings," "we are requesting the corps command and the RS Main Staff to appoint a competent person to solve the complex conflicts in the area in order to avoid the commander of the brigade appearing in front of the cameras." So General, if we go back to the war, this is a fair description of how you felt about UNPROFOR and its officers at the time, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations are mentioned separately here. I thought they had a mission, I thought they should be working and I thought their work was of mutual benefit; but there were various other individuals in groups that appeared for all sorts of reasons, exerting pressure both on the command and the troops, and making it impossible for us to do our job. That's why I wanted the corps command to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you are telling us that you are not referring to UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations as good-for-nothings?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Due to the bigger presence of UNPROFOR and different humanitarian organisations and other good-for-nothings ..."

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person who wrote this could have made this grammatical error, but that was not my thought. If one word applied to everyone, they wouldn't be listed separately. That word would be applied to all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So somebody else did this. But you must take credit or responsibility for the term "bitangi" coming out of your official reports to your superiors; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm responsible for the reports, especially if I was directly involved in their drafting. If I said to the operations duty officer what to write, using certain words and he put them in the way he saw fit, then this report might have gone out in this shape if I hadn't looked through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you heard when I asked Mr. Jevdjevic what happened to all the mosques in this area, and when I asked him who destroyed them. Do you remember what he said? I think he said idiots.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if that's what he said. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who destroyed the mosques in these areas that you liberated pursuant to this operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the axis of action of the Zvornik Brigade the only mosque we encountered was the one in Konjevic Polje and after the liberation of Konjevic Polje, the mosque remained intact. It stood as before but several days later, somebody destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your units helped move away the rubble, didn't they? You've seen the document.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That rubble, the remnants of the mosque stood there for a year or more, and I have seen documents showing that the corps commander or maybe even the Chief of Staff, Colonel Skocajic, ordered the command of the Zvornik Brigade, in brackets chief of engineering, to remove the rubble. And I believe it must have been pursuant to a request from someone from the government. Since that was not in my area, I tried to avoid that duty and I asked them for fuel. And this tug of war with the fuel lasted for a long time. But in any case, the rubble would have had to be removed. But my general position with regard to destruction of cultural and historical and other property is that it's not civilised. But if we want to be completely objective and realistic and we don't want to justify this kind of thing with the eye-for-an-eye theory, we still have to admit there was a cause-and-effect relationship in this destruction. The best thing, however, would be if all the Serbs listed their churches that were destroyed and all the Muslims listed their destroyed mosques and they helped each other rebuild those, that would be the best possible outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is the cause and the effect of the destruction of the mosques?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the effect is bad. We can talk a lot about causes. People are driven by all sorts of motives, and I believe that somebody who would be driven to destroy that mosque, would be somebody who used to have a house in that spot before that had been destroyed. And it's a frequent occurrence in Bosnia that churches and mosques replace each other at different intervals on the same foundations. It's not something to brag about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you suggest individual former residents as the main candidate for the destruction of these stone or concrete-reinforced buildings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Which mosques are we talking about? So far we've heard about one. Are there any more than Mr. McCloskey specifically wants to put to General Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can talk about Konjevic Polje, but the General and I know that the mosques in this area were destroyed and that's what we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What area, the whole of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The area of the operation of -- of Proboj. I can go through the mosques but I don't want to spend the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we know exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think if we can stick with Konjevic Polje, I think that's a good representative sample. And I don't think anyone is going to suggest anything differently on what happened to the mosques in all of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, General, are you suggesting former local residents as the most likely candidate for destroying the Konjevic Polje mosque, for example?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that such people may have a motive to do that. However, when I was leaving Konjevic Polje, the mosque was still standing. Who destroyed it later, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've heard the news recently on the mosques in Banja Luka and the Republika Srpska taking responsibilities for that; one of those was a UNESCO heritage site. Does that suggest to you that this might have been an organised situation from the top that led to the destruction of the Konjevic Polje mosque?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't understand that question. What news are we talking about and how is somebody who is in prison supposed to hear the news and on what medium. Perhaps put a document to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't know about this piece of news either. I mean, we only know what we hear and see in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he doesn't know anything about it, he can't answer the question, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you shouldn't put a question on a news item that is not in the records. I mean, I follow -- at least I speak for myself, but I've always been taught to follow the principle of quod non est in actis, non est in mundo, whatever is not in the records, does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a good faith belief in the event that I spoke of and it's directly responsive to him suggesting that it's villagers doing it. But I will go on. There's enough bad news in the news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know the news that I'm talking about either?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You tell him he can't ask the question and he asks it. I mean, it's disrespectful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 4286. Excuse me, let me cancel that. Let's go to 65 ter 4288.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this, we can see, is dated 24 February 1994, from the Drina Corps, entitled "Removal of the remains of the destroyed mosque in Konjevic Polje." Order. And it is to the Zvornik Brigade and it orders you to: "To use mechanical equipment of the engineering company of your brigade to start immediately with of the removal of the remains of the destroyed mosque in Konjevic Polje. The remains of the mosque are to be dumped at the closest site for disposal of waste material." So, is this the order that you were talking about earlier, that your brigade got, you remember this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go to 65 ter 4289. And it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am sorry for interrupting you, Mr. McCloskey, but we have a technical problem. I was just trying to find out if it's only temporary or whether it would be better to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's wait a little bit. Someone has got a mobile in here and I just heard the beep of an SMS being just received. Was it a watch?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I think the problem is a little bit more serious than we originally thought. It requires some time. So let's have a break. 25 minutes. If it's not solved until then, of course we'll let you know but the break is of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, we were at that point where we saw a document that the Drina Corps was ordering you, your brigade, to go clean up the rubble from the mosque. How was it that the Zvornik Brigade got tasked with a mosque in Konjevic Polje, which as we know is closer to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time there was the 5th -- if the 5th Engineering Battalion was in Konjevic Polje was there at the time, they would have been given this task. However, the Drina Corps believed that the Zvornik Brigade had more machinery at their disposal and for that reason they assigned this task to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And several months earlier, the Zvornik Brigade had actually liberated Konjevic Polje; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a few months. Eleven months before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, as you know, we found three documents where you were requesting fuel. Let me just go to the last one which is 65 ter 4291, which was dated 28 February. The other two were dated, respectively, 24 February at 65 ter 4289, and 25 February, 65 ter 4290. But let's just go to this last one to save some time at 4291. And it's probably best just to leave it on the screen. You can see down at number 9 you are requesting: "We are again requesting 300 hundred litres of petrol to remove the remaining parts of the mosque." So did you finally get that job done?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to avoid doing this job and whenever someone from the corps command asked to inquiry whether we had done it, we used fuel as an excuse. I believe that ultimately all this debris was removed by the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's get into 1995. There's been a lot of time spent -- you have spent a lot of time being questioning and answering on that so I don't expect to go through all of that in the kind of detail they went through, I don't think that's necessary. But I do want to go through a few things. You recall what you said about Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go to 65 ter 203, which is the Drina Corps document dated 20 of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which, as you've already said, was the Drina Corps taking the Directive 7 and adapting it to operations for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 6 in the English, and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is under the section entitled, "The tasks of the Drina Corps," but as you've stated out, before the section on the tasks of the units. And it's that now famous or infamous language I want to ask you about. "By planned and well thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." What does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this trial, this has been extensively discussed and I talked at length about this during my examination-in-chief. As I understand it, the Srebrenica enclave was created because the 28th Division was not demilitarised and removed from the area, but rather, by means of its combat deployment, managed to create this completely isolated enclave in geographical and demographic sense. What the author of this sentence had in mind I can only guess. I already said that the main culprit for this grave situation that the residents of the Zepa enclave had to suffer was the 28th Division, that there was a rift between the political and military leaderships within the zone itself, and that the VRS tried to deepen this rift in order to defeat those who wanted to continue fighting, and for this enclave to cease to be an enclave and that people could live there normally. There's another type of combat activities that can be understood to be implied in this sentence, and that is the so-called sabotage, psychological and propaganda activities aimed at undermining the morale of people, manpower of the enemy causing anxiety and insecurity and that can be achieved through propaganda, media, leaflets, radio broadcasts, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, this says, "By planned and well thought-out combat operations," and goes on. I won't repeat it. Is this targeting the civilian populations of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was the idea, it would have been worded thus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't take the words "create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." So you don't take the term for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa to involve the population?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local population are civilians. There was an attempt from inside to persuade or to make the political military leadership inside Srebrenica to stop treating them as their prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you read this as a target of the civilian population by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is now a new question. Taking the civilians by the Serbs as a target, that's not it. It was possible to expose them to propaganda so that they would act and exert influence on the authorities, military and civilian. If the 28th Division had not been there, there wouldn't have been any VRS units deployed around the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I take it you don't see anything wrong or illegal or militarily inappropriate in this phrase?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the sentence itself is phrased in such a way that it can involve various connotations, primarily some that are contrary to the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, just for your better understanding of what is going to happen. Next break will be at 11.50. 11.50. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I'm not asking for an academic or professorial answer. I need your military opinion as a General. And is there anything wrong with this phrase, in your view?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is, of course. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sentence that says -- I myself don't see any reason to create unbearable conditions for the population in order to achieve a military objective. Perhaps that was an indirect attempt to somehow exert pressure or impact on the 28th Division. But I wouldn't like to go back to that. This is not a precedent in wars. Things like this happened before and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that -- I don't think I'll ask any more questions on that. Now, let's go back to a document, 65 ter 2920. This is dated 25 April 1995, about a month or so after this last document. This is the document involving "poturice." I do not want to get into that topic again. But what I want to ask you about is the message, the specific message that I have identified here. If we look at page 1 of the English and the B/C/S, there's three particular segments I want to draw your attention to. The first is right at the top: "The moment has come when the issue of liberating the Serbian lands from poturice will be finally resolved in this area by resolute and successful action of our forces." And we go down a little further in the paragraph: "They," meaning the Muslims, "have given us a unique chance to push them away from us for all time as they are asking for it and put them under control in this area." And we go down to the next paragraph: "The adequate response of our forces meant that we realised that there would be no peace and security in Semberija and Donje Podrinje until the poturice were completely defeated and driven out of this area." These three statements are similar in idea to what we saw in Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not similar at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That by planned and well thought-out combat operations create total insecurity, which was announcing the idea of directing operations against the Muslims at this time-frame. Now we see, coming out of your house, the idea that it is now time to defeat the Muslims, the poturice, to]get them out of the area. These are similar ideas, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not similar are ideas. If you look at the date when this information was compiled, that was during the Operation Spreca. Before that, truce had been signed that lasted for nearly 3 months; then this was breached by the Muslim forces launching an offensive. We had to respond to this offensive. I don't know how many of these truces were agreed and then breached. Therefore, if we understand that the objective of the Muslim leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina was to create a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina dominated by the Islamic authorities, the Serbs had to defend themselves from that. We had no other choice. Nobody wanted to drive Muslims from Bosnia or that Serbs should leave Bosnia. We are still living there in this area and we will have to continue to live, but on condition that everybody's rights are respected. This is the issue of identity. Nothing more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So making life impossible for the civilians of Srebrenica and Zepa is in no way related to the idea of liberating Serbian lands from "poturice"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims still live in Srebrenica to this date, so obviously that was not the objective. The objective was to make them realise that there was no life for them as long as the 28th Division was there, and living in the enclave. If the 28th Division wasn't there, they would have been living like everybody else in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you think General Mladic would have allowed the Muslims to stay living in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what he would have done, whether it was up to him to decide or not. But I remember during the preparation for Dayton negotiations aimed at ending the era in Bosnia, the Serbian proposal was for all these enclaves, Srebrenica, Zepa and other, remain as they were, where they were and to be given to the Muslims once the issue of division of territories was on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 4256.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is again another document involving "poturices," but I want to ask you to take a look at -- it's page 2 in the English, it's right near the end in the B/C/S, the second paragraph up. And it states: "The task of the Zvornik Brigade is that in coordination with other forces 'finish off' poturices at Zecija Kosa and Vitinica and crash all poturices' illusions that they are going to stay there." Now this is another document that you have acknowledged was yours and these areas of - pardon the pronunciation - Zecija Kosa and Vitinica, were they part of the Spreca operation.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are pronouncing the names of these features perfectly. Zecija Kosa is a mountain and -- as well as Visoko Glava. This is where the frontline was and this is where fighting took place. This is where we defeated their forces. It has nothing to do with residents of Teocak, Tuzla, Kalesija or anyone else. This refers to those fighters with whom we were engaged in combat and this is information that speaks about combat successes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So "all poturices" only means combat soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this word was used and refer -- it was used to refer to those who acted in the same way as, back in history, the Ottoman empire did by forcing Christians to convert. All these who subscribe to this very same idea during this war, that's how we called them. That included Alija as well and he didn't hide it. He spoke about that and wrote about that publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on. On page 30809 of the transcript, you said in regard to convoys: "The brigade didn't have any powers to either allow or reject the passage of convoys. The people who manned checkpoints were only to act in compliance with the usual procedure upon receiving a notice that a convoy was coming and to check the contents of what they were carrying." So your brigade did follow the orders related to convoys and just followed the orders? You didn't act on your own in any way?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and both if we were to let a convoy pass through or halt it, depending on the order that we received and we would act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that procedure was one by the Drina Corps and the Main Staff with you following their orders?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood that this chain went from the Main Staff via a corps down to the brigades. Later on, we saw that that was expanded to the state level when this coordinating body became involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Just one document on this point. Exhibit 5D 00321.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 4 April 1995, one of your reports to the Drina Corps command. If you could just go to page 2 in the B/C/S, page 2 of the English. Under your name, several domestic goods were confiscated, shampoo, detergents, towels. This was a vehicle with two persons in it. Cigarettes. Sir, did you receive orders to confiscate that material from these two people going to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly did because if we did this on our own, we wouldn't have reported it. This is a report from us about what we did concerning the order that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 107, which is a familiar document that you have spoken about. I won't spend too much time with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is the attack plan for Srebrenica, dated 2 July, by General Zivanovic. If we could go to page 3 in the English, and page 2 in the B/C/S under paragraph 2. Paragraph number 2. And we see here that: "The command of the Drina Corps pursuant to operations Directive 7 and 7/1, and on the basis of the situation in the corps area of responsibility, has the task of carrying out offensive activities with free forces deep in the Drina Corps zone, as soon as possible, in order to split apart the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, and reduce them to their urban areas." At the time what did you think that meant, "reduce them to their urban areas"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I knew that they had to be divided, meaning that we had to cut off any communication between Zepa and Srebrenica, between the Zepa Brigade and the forces in Srebrenica. Secondly, based on the agreement on militarisation, the borders of the enclave were not clearly defined, and there were some disputes between the signatories to the agreement. In my mind, the urban area included the centre of the town and the surrounding settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the surrounding settlements in the countryside that we've all been to, you consider to be the urban area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, speaking about an enclave, I stick to -- my understanding was that the positions of the 28th Division should have been pushed to the line that I mentioned. It was them who created the enclave, not the people who lived in various locations and villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have been through that, I don't want to go through it again. But I would like an answer to my question. You consider the countryside and the villages around Srebrenica town to be part of the urban area; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not hamlets or villages, but suburbs, and the tasks show which line the units had to reach and this is much farther than the suburb area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last three names of the settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need you to repeat the last three names of the settlement, please, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The line that units participating in active operations throughout Srebrenica were to reach were Alibegovac, Kak, Zivkovo Brdo and Rajine. These were the features that are far away from the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what did they have to do with the urban area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't have been possible or purposeful from the military tactical aspect to move the frontline of the VRS to the urban area of the town. The positions would have been unviable. These positions that I quoted give you a possibility of a effective defence and the possibility to push the 28th Division out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't think this order really meant urban area, you think it meant the perimeter of the objectives that were laid out in the order?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the author said reduce the enclaves to their urban areas, and then he specified to which lines the units were to go. It's not the same, those lines the units were supposed to take, and the urban area. The urban area is not just the town. The urban area also includes suburbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Suburbs of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the entrance to Srebrenica, before the Domavija hotel there, is a village that practically continues into the town. You have Potocari village which practically flows into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You are suggesting the urban area referred to in this document is this area within the perimeter of the defined tasks?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you which positions the VRS were supposed to take, to reach. Anything outside that closer to Srebrenica town, would have been the area where the 28th Division was active, and the population lived. That is, as opposed to the urban area mentioned in paragraph 2 of this order. You see, even the author of this text was not very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it's the position of Prosecutor that the author of this text knew exactly what he was doing. Let me ask you -- you don't agree with that, but let me ask you -- the people, you were aware that there were thousands of refugees living in the Srebrenica enclave both inside the town and in the villages outside the town; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that people were living there. How many, I didn't know, because I was not interested. I was not studying that area. But if we applied that to the urban part of the town knowing what Srebrenica is like, then all these people would have been driven out into the street because there's only one main street and two cross streets. What would have that been like?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, my question was, you knew that there were refugees living in and around Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, he answered it. Line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I think he has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "I knew that people were living there." Of course people were living there. I want to know about refugees. There's a very big difference in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just because he doesn't give you the answer you want, doesn't mean he hasn't answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have to agree with that and we have too. On the other hand, he has made it clear now that he is making a clear distinction between people in general and refugees in particular, and he is seeking a direct response from your client on that particular category of people. So, Mr. Pandurevic, if you could answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, Your Honour. Refugees are also part of the population that lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, General, I didn't spend a day talking about 1993 just because we had documents. Many of the refugees that were living in Srebrenica in July 1995 were actually refugees from the area that we saw on the map that used to be behind you; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I agree with you. I would even say the same is true of the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As the frontlines varied and moved, the population on both or, rather, all three warring sides moved back and forth, and Srebrenica is no exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you could anticipate, with the combat actions you engaged in pursuant to this operation, that the Muslim populations would move away from your forces into the town?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even that could be anticipated and such things did happen. And when the moment came to carry out a demilitarisation of that area and to make Srebrenica an open town, meaning that all military installations, moveable and immovable, should have been removed, making it a purely civilian territory. If that had been done, that population would have been left alone to live there to this day. However, the signatories of the agreement did not honour the agreement and the resulting situation we all know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you say, "even that could be anticipated," did you anticipate that happening at the time of the attack, that the Muslims would move away into the town? You yourself?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that they would flee into the town. The civilian population needed to be removed from the zone of combat operations. An agreement between warring sides could have created special safe areas where the population could have been removed for the duration of combat activities. However, this does not happen in this war. The sides could not agree about that. And my attempts were geared at temporarily removing the population from the area for the duration of combat activities. They pulled out together with their troops. However, when the safe area was created, if the demilitarisation had been created behind Serb lines, there would have been no military units and all that population would have been able to live normally. The frontline would have been facing only the 28th Corps. However, the Muslim army didn't want it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you acknowledge that it was part of your objective to remove the civilian population from the area, but so that they could be safe and that they could come back and live in harmony with their brothers and sisters?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply, you can use your deduction and try to reach that conclusion based on my answers. I don't see how that can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just I want to point out a couple of other things which I think you will agree with me on. We should still be on that page 3 in English, page 2 in the B/C/S. It goes down on paragraph 4 in the B/C/S and at the end of it, after talking about improving the tactical positions and providing certain trig points, that to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves. What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- actually follows up on my previous answer. To improve a tactical position means the following: Almost a half of the Drina Corps should be pulled out from this area and should be geared towards the 2nd Corps. Reduce frontline, and jeopardize the 2nd Corps militarily. It doesn't mean deploying forces around the enclaves and using three or four brigades to keep the position. That's what improving military position means. Elimination of enclaves does not mean elimination of the population, it means eliminating the 28th Division which made up the enclave basically. The safe area and the enclave is not the same thing. And you can't find a provision in international law where --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is lost, I'm sorry, can we have a repetition of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, the interpreters had a problem. The last we have in the transcript is the following: "... and you can't find a provision in international law where." And you need to continue from there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It goes on to say, the international law of warfare, meaning the regulations we applied, know terms safe area and open town, but not enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Quick question. Do you think that between the 11th of July and the 15th of July, that the VRS was following the international rule of law that you've just mentioned, or can we agree that that was pretty much put on the shelf for a few days?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat your words when you said that an attack on the enclave was a legitimate military target. A quick response to a quick question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So elimination of the enclaves doesn't mean elimination of the enclaves. It means defeating the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What needed to be done was to demilitarise the area completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I'm not asking what needed to be done. I'm just trying to clarify your last answer. Let me try again. So you are saying elimination of the enclaves means defeating the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Disarming and demilitarising the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go over to page 3 in the B/C/S, page 5 in the English. After discussing various tasks of various units, it says: "In case of the advantageous development of the situation, be in readiness for an attack and pursuit of the enemy along the aforementioned axes." That particular line was meant for everyone involved in this operation, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Could you answer it, please, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't found in my text the passage just read by Mr. McCloskey. Can I get a reference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In B/C/S, Mr. McCloskey said it's on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, it's page 3, B/C/S; page 5, English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's under paragraph 5 but it's a long paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It begins, the paragraph: "The first Milici Brigade has the task of reaching the area of," da da da da da. And it's a new paragraph and it says: "In case of advantageous development of the situation, be in readiness for an attack and pursuit of the enemy along the aforementioned axes." Was that only referring to the Milici Brigade or was that -- should all units be ready to do that should the opportunity arise?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's defined here as a task for the Milici Brigade but if we interpret this in the context of some tactical standards and procedures, then always when the opportunity arises in combat to pursue the enemy, then you move from the phase of attack to the phase of pursuit. In this case, it means pursuing military units, no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You heard the testimony about that mortar round that landed right in the middle of the crowd that was gathered around the Dutch Battalion base in Srebrenica. What do you know about that? Who fired that round into that crowd?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that shell just as much as I heard during the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing more?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You also heard that as the Muslim population was moving along the road in massive numbers from Srebrenica to Potocari, rounds were falling on either side of the road. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as in my previous answer about the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go now to the meeting in Bratunac that you have testified was on 11 July. I think you understand the Prosecution's position is that that occurred on the 12th of July. And you likely recall from your review of the Krstic case that General Krstic also said this meeting occurred on the 11th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall what Mr. Krstic said about that meeting, but in the documents that you have shown us, I have seen testimony by a Dutch officer, I believe it was Koster Edres [phoen], Mr. Petrusic had asked him about that date and he was probably talking about the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was and I can ask you a bit about that a bit later. I just wants to make sure that you've had a chance to review the material on this topic and that as you sit here today you are absolutely sure that it was on the 11th, not the 12th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade on the 11th of July at 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was Mr. Jevdjevic there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Mr. Jevdjevic at one point. I don't know what happened to him later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have the fish dinner with him or know about the famous fish dinner, Mr. Bajagic, I think, made. We are talking about the same night?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that famous dinner. There was a simple ordinary dinner, a short one after the meeting, and I was there. The dinner was prepared and brought by Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it was fish?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of fish?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know much about fish, a river fish, a sea fish, but the dish was called drunken carp. A carp prepared specially in wine, and I know that the carp is a freshwater fish. That much I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Beara at that dinner?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If it had been sea fish, maybe he would have attended, but he did not attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Jevdjevic said that Mr. Furtula was in Bratunac that night on the 11th. Do you agree with him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Furtula in Srebrenica, but as for the meeting in Bratunac, I don't recall him being there so I can't say either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me show you a clip to see if this is the person you are talking about, and it's from the trial video which I should know the 65 ter number by now, but. We are at 00:30:00:3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that person over General Mladic's left shoulder, is that the guy you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's Mr. Radomir Furtula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's the same Furtula that was mentioned, as far as you know, in the conversation between Colonel Beara and General Zivanovic on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that referred to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this meeting on 11th, I believe Mr. Jevdjevic described that you had made comments about General Mladic's order to go to Zepa the next day, that you spoke up a bit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that trial video is 2047. All right. And I just -- I will try to do this briefly, but I want to go over some of the evidence of the date of that meeting. You have had a chance to see the intercept that we discussed with Mr. Jevdjevic when he was here that the Prosecution has said happened at 1850 hours, and that Mr. Jevdjevic said, We are going to be at bottom now, extension 385, and you can reach bottom via Zlatar 1. Okay. Do you remember that conversation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember you questioned Mr. Jevdjevic about these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you remember that he said that take place but it didn't take place on the 12th, but that it took place one day earlier on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember his testimony that he associated his activities, these ones, with the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review the intercepts to determine if the date is as Mr. Jevdjevic said it, or as the Prosecution says it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the printed version of that intercept, the date 12th is quoted, but I don't think there is a date in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you have had a chance to look at the notebook version and see the intercepts on either side of the notebook and what they are talking about and see the date of the 13th in the notebook right before this intercept; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it might be better for you to show me the notebook again because I think there are no dates for a period of 7 to 8 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I should have said the date of the 13th was right after the intercept in question, not before, if I misspoke. Well, General, I don't think I'm going to take the time to go through that. We went through with Mr. Jevdjevic and I don't think I'm going to change your mind from those intercepts. But I did wanted to ask you if you had a chance to review them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you just let me know the intercept number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 4262. And Your Honours, I can go over that if you would like me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, same position here. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not even necessary, at the end of the day. I can give you some other opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, have you heard what the witness said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me for turning my back, General. Yes, and we'll have a chance to go over your other opinions. I don't want to dwell on these intercept, I think they speak for themselves, and I don't think we're going to find agreement. I just wanted to give the General a chance to change his mind and be open to the possibility that he is mistaken. Which apparently you are not, right, General?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't understand cross-examination as a personal communication between you and me. I understand it as something that is supposed to be for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. I want to tell you my own view. We see in the notebook that the dates are missing for several day. We have conversations, one after another, written in different handwriting, meaning different persons wrote them down, and the question logically arises in my mind, were all these intercepts recorded by one device and one tape in sequence? Were they recorded on several devices on several tapes and then several operators noted them down? Or maybe one person recorded it and another noted it down. And perhaps the person who recorded it in the first place did not record the frequency or the date. I cannot agree with you that the contents of the conversation alone can tell us the date. It can tell us about the activities and the area. And one more thing. Although Jevdjevic is a better expert than I am, the bearing is the same on the 15th and the 12th, and Jevdjevic was certainly in Krivace on the 15th and he could have hardly been on the same place on the 12th, and we have the same bearing for the 12th and the 15th, which is 135.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you've taken me into it. I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the number you gave me is the number of the note. Do you have the 65 ter number of that specific intercept you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. I will go through that intercept, but I also get you that reference, one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the notebook, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, for you it would be the ERN ending 7909 and it's page 5 in the English translation. And we see in the handwriting on the left side, and this is 4087 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 4087, Judge Kwon, for the -- independent of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we look at these intercepts, we can see the intercept at 1850 hours. And we are in 65 ter 4262 for -- sorry about the confusion, I don't know any way of doing this. And we can see that intercept and that's the one between Major Jevdjevic and the switchboard. Now, if we go back in time from 1850, General, the one before that is at 1310, and it says: "About five or six buses are coming down. They should be refueled with 25 litres each until Han Pijesak." That doesn't tell -- to me that doesn't tell me much, buses are being fueled and going places. But let's look at the next one at 1250. Someone is asking about Radomir, that doesn't tell us much. Then if we go to 1205, there's a conversation and I think we can look at this and it says at the end of the conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the booklet that we have been provided with it's the English translation page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it says: "Brane --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to make sure that the accused are following? Do you have -- okay. Thank you. Proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Brane said they are collecting trucks and buses to drive from Srebrenica and they are going to load 300 in each." Now, at 1205 on the 11th of July, Srebrenica hadn't even fallen yet, so that can't have occurred on 11 July, agreed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you that based on the contents of the intercepts one can recognise events going on in the field, and since we know the sequence of events shall then it's all right. However, we are seeing here various entries in this notebook and I would like to repeat what I said earlier. We don't know when these conversations were written down from the tape. Maybe this was done on the 11th. You have a typed version mentioning the word "bearing," whereas in the handwritten version there's no mentioning of the bearing.
